verdict.reason: Val Kilmer's vocal mimicry is genuinely uncanny and worth hearing in a theater, but Stone's approach is more fever dream than biography, so manage expectations for narrative coherence. The 140-minute runtime asks a lot for a film that often prioritizes spectacle over insight.

ratings.plot: A young girl new to a Catholic school befriends a coven of witches whom the other students either shun or fear. But when a powerful invocation goes wrong, the consequences could endanger their lives.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're in the mood for '90s goth camp that hasn't aged well outside of nostalgia. The execution is uneven and it plays better as a streaming rewatch than a theater commitment.

ratings.plot: When Casey Connor, Herrington High School's newspaper photographer, witnesses the murder of a nurse and sees her alive again, he decides to investigate the bizarre happenings.

verdict.reason: Skip it if you want Rodriguez firing on all cylinders, but catch it if you're in the mood for late-90s B-movie energy and don't mind uneven tone. The film swings wildly between genuine scares and comedy, held together by Rodriguez's visual flair but undermined by a script that can't quite commit to either register.

ratings.plot: When a rogue squad of genetically engineered super soldiers break loose in the desert, a badass Army sniper must unleash hell to protect her young daughter.

verdict.reason: Adam Wingard knows how to stage action sequences with real clarity and momentum, but the premise is thin and the execution lands somewhere between competent and forgettable. Catch it at Alamo Drafthouse if you want the social viewing experience, otherwise wait for streaming.

ratings.plot: A violent police detective investigates a brutal murder that might involve a manipulative and seductive novelist.

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's 1992 pulp is sleek, nasty, and fun in ways that feel genuinely transgressive, but it's also hollow beneath the surface seduction. The Alamo screenings honor its B-movie ambitions if you're in the mood for camp with edge.

ratings.plot: An adaptation of Homer's great epic, the film follows the assault on Troy by the united Greek forces.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical experience unless you're committed to seeing a baggy, uneven epic on 35mm film at Metrograph. The 163-minute runtime and narrative sprawl work better compressed at home, but the restoration print is worth the trip if you're already downtown and have the time.

ratings.plot: After her mother commits suicide, a young woman travels to Italy in search of love, truth and a deeper connection with herself.

verdict.reason: Bertolucci's uneven chamber piece has genuine moments of visual grace, but the film's reach exceeds its grasp and the pacing sags in its second half. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, which makes the Tuscan light worth seeing large, though streaming at home won't hurt you.

ratings.plot: In April 1964, more than twenty years after the Nazis won World War II, S.S. officer Xavier March uncovers a plot to eliminate the attendees of the Wannsee Conference so that Germany can establish better relations with the U.S.

verdict.reason: A fumbled alternate-history thriller that wastes its premise, but the 1994 HBO production has enough production design and Rutger Hauer's weary performance to justify a single viewing at Lincoln Center if you're committed to exploring '90s speculative television. The film's earnest mid-budget craft—swallowing the clumsy narrative—holds up better on a theater screen than it would on a small one.

ratings.plot: A classic tale about bitter relationships between a frivolous girl and a soldier is adapted for the post-World War II time.

verdict.reason: Clouzot's adaptation has genuine power but arrives uneven and padded at 100 minutes. The Film at Lincoln Center restoration makes this the only way to see it properly on a big screen, and the post-war Paris setting carries real historical weight if you're willing to sit with the film's tonal shifts.

verdict.reason: Skip the multiplexes, but catch it at Alamo Drafthouse if you're in the mood for midnight-movie chaos and don't mind sitting through an uneven pitch. Bousman swings wildly between genuine visual invention and tonal whiplash, but the opera-horror-splatter hybrid commitment is rare enough to warrant one viewing in a room built for cult movies.

ratings.plot: On vacation in Thailand, Richard sets out for an island rumored to be a solitary beach paradise.

verdict.reason: Boyle's visual ambition salvages a thin premise, but the film indulges its own hype and outstays its welcome. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the digital palette that defined late-90s blockbuster excess, which is worth seeing once on a large screen.

ratings.plot: Nicolas, the eldest son of a wealthy family, works far from his home environment as a window washer and dishwasher in a bistro. He does not notice at all the baseness of his new relationships.

verdict.reason: Iosseliani's gentle comedies reward patience, but this 1999 film sits between his strongest work and risks feeling slight on a single viewing. The Metrograph DCP gives the provincial French settings clarity, though the 118-minute runtime and episodic structure demand the right mood.

The 88-minute runtime is forgiving, and Breien's approach to female friendship and domestic life has aged better than most '80s fare.

Metrograph's DCP restoration shows off the neon-soaked cinematography and fight choreography that justifies the theatrical setting.

ratings.plot: David Lynch cemented his reputation as an uncompromising visionary with BLUE VELVET, one of the most controversial films of the 1980s, burrowing beneath the surface of idyllic suburban America to reveal a sinister underworld of sex and violence. After stumbling upon a severed human ear, a young college student (Kyle MacLachlan) becomes obsessed with investigating its origins and gets entangled with a nightclub chanteuse (Isabella Rossellini) and her psychopathic lover (Dennis Hopper). A masterfully eerie, depraved psychosexual nightmare and one of the greatest films of the 1980s. “Frank Booth is the role Dennis Hopper was born and chemically mutated to own. Sometimes David Lynch can teeter too far into the absurdity for absurdity's sake, but BLUE VELVET remains perfectly balanced as it dives into the dark, bizarre underbelly of society that lurks just below the surface of suburbia. It is also worth noting that BLUE VELVET, when screened in the first month of operation at the original Alamo, was the movie that inspired our strict no-talking policy.” ( Tim League, Alamo Drafthouse founder)

One of the most derided movies of the 20th century is also one of its most spectacularly misunderstood. The odd-couple tag team of Dutch provocateur director Paul Verhoeven (ROBOCOP, ELLE) and Sleazoid-Hungarian-American writer Joe Eszterhas (FLASHDANCE, SLIVER) first came together with 1992's BASIC INSTINCT, and everyone, including the financial backers and the producer/distributors of this movie, assumed lightning would strike twice for the duo with 1995's SHOWGIRLS. Universally panned by critics upon its initial release, people found the multi-tap combo of inane dialogue, wild over-acting, and extreme obscenity and grotesquerie to be just too much. Then the "so-bad-it's-good" crowd sunk their hollow claws into the movie, claiming it as one of the "best worst" movies of all time. To be sure, yes, this is a movie in which Saved By the Bell 's Elizabeth Berkley sets fire to her TV-star image by grinding her pelvis on Kyle MacLachlan's lap until he simulates sexual climax while Gina Gershon watches. She shoves chips into her mouth and reminisces about her days of eating and enjoying "puppy chow," between bouts of trying to make it as a Las Vegas showgirl "goddess." The assumption that critics and chuckleheads alike have made are that a) Verhoeven and Eszterhas weren't trying to make something with humor (they were), and b) that the surface story is meant to be taken at face value (it's not). Verhoemie don't play that. SHOWGIRLS is a complicated, satirical masterpiece that tests the audience's limits of empathy and challenges some basic assumptions about American dreams of celebrity, pokes at the artificiality of Hollywood glitz and glamour, and shines a light on the misogyny and dehumanization inherent in the entertainment industry, all while keeping the audiences on their toes as they try to know whether they should laugh, cry, or scratch their heads because there are random interruptions by chimpanzees and the fiercest dancing ever committed to celluloid. (Laird Jimenez)

Bring your whole coven to Alamo Drafthouse and see what kind of trouble the Owens sisters get into this time.

verdict.reason: The Filipino folklore angle and friendship-stakes premise have real weight, but a 109-minute animated film built on a farewell story lands harder at home than in a theater full of strangers. DreamWorks polish can't overcome the fact that intimate emotional beats don't need the big screen.

ratings.plot: A former Army Special Forces soldier and his retired combat dog attempt to return to civilization after suffering a catastrophic accident deep in the Alaskan wilderness.

verdict.reason: David Ayer brings reliable action craft to a survival story, but the premise is thin and the runtime suggests he hasn't found enough meat for the theater. See it at Alamo Drafthouse if you want a comfortable seat and don't mind waiting for home video.

ratings.plot: After a seven-year hiatus following the devastating loss of their beloved bandmate Chester Bennington, Linkin Park's remaining members struggle to find their way forward. Their shared history and enduring friendship, combined with the fresh perspective of two new band members, spark a renewed creative energy that leads them on a transformative journey of artistic reinvention. Following the band from intimate 2022 studio sessions through their explosive From Zero album release and concert in São Paulo, the film UNSHATTER weaves together rare vault footage, electrifying performances from sold-out shows, and candid interviews with band members and fans – capturing the raw, honest story of what it means to start over.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical run unless you need the crowd energy; this is a band documentary that works fine on a screen at home. The 107-minute runtime and concert footage don't demand a theater seat the way a live performance does.

ratings.plot: Desperate to save what is left of his family, during the height of the Great Depression, a battle-scarred veteran is hired to help smuggle a fortune in gold across 100 miles of impenetrable wilderness.

verdict.reason: This Depression-era survival story has craft and mood, but the premise leans familiar and the runtime tests patience for a film built on single-location tension. The live Q&A sweetens the deal if you want to engage directly with the filmmakers after the screening.

ratings.plot: Shrouded in secrecy! Encircled by intrigue! The Mystery Machine promises to deliver cinematic treasures that span genres, countries, and tastes... only for those brave enough to enter. All shall be revealed only after the credits begin. Screening on select Mondays with discounted admission.

verdict.reason: A blind screening can be fun if you trust the programmer and have time to burn on a Monday night. Alamo Drafthouse's track record with these events is solid, but you're paying for surprise over certainty, and that gamble only pays off if you're in the mood for it.

ratings.plot: 40 YEARS OF FUCKIN' UP is SPINAL TAP, but real. It's a film about the infamous, fairly unfamous, and beloved punk rock band NOFX. This is the unbelievable story about how a group of untalented, drug-addicted teenage punks somehow became the most successful independent band in history – and they did it haphazardly, entirely on their own.

verdict.reason: A chaotic, fun ride for NOFX devotees and punk history buffs, but the two-hour-plus runtime tests even true believers. The Alamo's beer-and-heckle atmosphere is the right venue for this kind of controlled mess, which matters more than the film itself.

movies.title: The Twilight Saga: New Moon Fan Screening

ratings.plot: The supernatural tale of star-crossed lovers continues as the Cullen family flees Forks in order to protect Bella (Kristen Stewart), and the heartbroken high-school senior discovers that vampires aren't the only creatures in town. Realizing that Bella will never be safe as long as he's around, Edward (Robert Pattinson) makes the difficult decision to leave his beloved behind shortly after her 18th birthday. Reeling from her loss, Bella embraces self-destruction after being comforted by Edward's image during a moment of mortal peril. But as heavy-hearted as Bella may be, her friend Jacob (Taylor Lautner) distracts her from her sorrows by helping her renovate a weather-beaten motorbike. When Bella encounters a former adversary with a sizable grudge, she's rescued from harm at the last second by a pack of enormous, ferocious wolves. Subsequently delving into the history of the Quileutes, Bella discovers the secrets of Jacob's tribe while looking forward to a reunion with Edward that may have deadly consequences.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical trip unless you're committed to the communal fan experience at Alamo Drafthouse. The film itself plays better at home, and a 131-minute runtime demands comfort you won't find in a movie theater seat.

ratings.plot: TWILIGHT is an action-packed, modern-day love story between a teen girl and a vampire. Bella Swan (Kristen Stewart) has always been a bit different, never fitting in with the girls at her school. When Bella is sent to live with her father in the rainy little town of Forks, Washington, she doesn’t expect much to change. Then she meets the mysterious and dazzlingly beautiful Edward Cullen (Robert Pattinson), a boy unlike any she’s ever met. Edward is a vampire, but he doesn’t have fangs and his family is unique in that they choose not to drink human blood. Edward has been waiting 90 years for a soul mate, which he finds in Bella. They are soon swept up in a passionate and unorthodox romance. Edward must struggle to resist the primal pull of her scent, which could send him into an uncontrollable frenzy, but what will they do when a clan of new vampires – James (Cam Gigandet), Laurent (Edi Gathegi), and Victoria (Rachelle Lefevre) – come to town and threaten to disrupt their way of life?

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical trip unless you're in the mood for nostalgic communal viewing with fellow fans. The Alamo Drafthouse screenings trade theatrical immersion for crowd energy, which is the only reason to leave home for a film better experienced alone or streaming.

ratings.plot: “If I didn’t know Jodi Wille’s film was a documentary, I’d swear it was a WTF, insane, sci-fi tale of weirdness.” —Film Threat “Absolutely riveting.” —Nova Religio “A vision of healing, acceptance, peace, cooperation, and hope, expressed through an outpouring of unbridled creative energy.” —Artillery An up-close encounter with humankind: Jodi Wille (THE SOURCE FAMILY) lays bare the out-of-this-world true story of the Unarius Academy of Science, an extraterrestrial-loving spiritual sect, and their bedazzled leader, advanced clairvoyant Ruth E. Norman (aka Archangel Uriel), whose devotees transmitted their far-out message over public access television in 1980s Southern California. From producer Caryn Capotosto and Executive producers Elijah Wood, Phil Lord, and Christopher Miller.

movies.title: Verity HDR Early Access Girls Night Out

ratings.plot: Struggling writer Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) lands a seemingly easy ghostwriting job with famous author Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway), only to discover that the Crawford family has enough secrets to fill several bestselling thrillers. As she digs deeper into the disturbing autobiographical notes Verity has left behind, the line between fiction and reality starts getting seriously blurry, especially with Verity’s husband Jeremy (Josh Hartnett) in the picture. Based on Colleen Hoover’s bestselling novel and directed by Michael Showalter, VERITY is the kind of glossy, grown-up thriller that knows exactly how much fun it is to go off the rails.

verdict.reason: Skip the early access markup and catch this glossy Hoover adaptation on a regular screen when it opens wider; the HDR gimmick doesn't justify the Alamo premium for what is fundamentally a straightforward, entertaining thriller. Michael Showalter's direction prioritizes propulsive fun over anything that demands theatrical urgency, and the twists land just as well at home.

ratings.plot: From writer-director Bassam Tariq, YOUR MOTHER YOUR MOTHER YOUR MOTHER stars Mahershala Ali as Latif, a devoutly religious hitman who struggles to balance work, faith, and fatherhood. When his wife dies, he embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children, confronting the forces closing in around him – and the beliefs threatening to unravel within.
Widowed pear salesman Ernie Tyler travels to scatter his wife's ashes in places she specified, each location stirring memories that help him process their marriage, his work life, and his future.

verdict.reason: A modest indie comedy about grief that works best if you connect with Bruce Campbell's understated direction and the intimate pacing of a 90-minute road movie. The Alamo Drafthouse venues are solid but not a draw—this film has no theatrical urgency and plays just fine at home later.

movies.title: Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?

ratings.plot: Charting the Sheffield band’s extraordinary journey from obscurity to cultural touchstone. Fusing footage from Pulp’s biggest ever arena show – part of the global tour for ‘More’, the band’s first album in 24 years – with four decades of colourful, never-seen-before archival material.

verdict.reason: Essential for Pulp devotees, but a 99-minute concert doc plays better at home than in a theater built for food and chatter. The archival material is the real draw—unseen footage from four decades justifies the trip only if you're committed to the band's full story.

ratings.plot: Imagine that a local cable station was invaded by otherdimensional creatures at the stroke of midnight. That's Video Vortex. Each month, this series presents a mystery transmission that's culled from the outer limits of home video history – from essential underground films to surreal docs, from tokusatsu battle-parties to outsider experiments. So warm up the cathode tubes, dim the lights, and let your senses intermingle with the glow.

verdict.reason: A curated surprise screening works best if you trust the programmer's taste and have time to spare on an unknown 86-minute experience. The appeal lives entirely in the mystery itself and the venue's atmosphere, not in any film you can research beforehand.
